561.quote_or_event: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
561.explanation: When Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges King Nami to punish thieves and robbers to prove himself a true Kshatriya, Nami answers that human punishment is often misdirected.
561.tie_back: The Kural requires a king to investigate impartially before he punishes; Nami's reply names the injustice that follows when that inquiry is skipped.
561.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
561._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It warns against wrongful punishment but says nothing positive about proportion or preventing repetition.

562.quote_or_event: “He should not, in every case, wait for the express command (of the teacher) like an unbroken horse for the whip (of the rider), but like a broken horse which sees the whip (of the rider) he should commit no evil act.”
562.explanation: The first lecture on monastic discipline holds up the well-trained horse that needs only to see the whip, not feel it, as the model for a pupil.
562.tie_back: Valluvar's ruler raises the rod sternly but lets it fall gently; the Jain verse likewise says that the visible rod, not the blow, should be what keeps a well-disciplined person from wrongdoing.
562.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
562._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The verse is about a pupil and teacher, not a king and subjects, so the parallel is by analogy.

563.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
563.explanation: King Sanjaya, out hunting, kills the frightened deer in a park and then is himself seized with fear before the meditating monk Gardabhali, who tells him to give others the safety he wants for himself; the king renounces his throne.
563.tie_back: The Kural says a king who habitually fills his people with dread will swiftly perish; the Jain story makes the same point from inside, showing the inflicter of fear becoming afraid and being told to give up cruelty and grant safety (abhaya) instead.
563.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 18.11 (with 18.3-10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
563._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close in spirit, but the king's cruelty here is to animals in a hunt, not to his subjects.

564.quote_or_event: “As a bitch with sore ears is driven away everywhere, thus a bad, insubordinate, and talkative (pupil) is turned out.”
564.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana warns that a person whose conduct makes him disliked is rejected wherever he goes.
564.tie_back: The Kural's king earns the people's bitter name 'cruel' and is cut off; in the Jain verse too, a reputation for bad conduct leads to rejection.
564.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
564._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. This is a weak next-best match: it concerns a disobedient pupil, not a harsh ruler, and has nothing about a shortened life or reign.

565.quote_or_event: Jain tradition holds that after attaining omniscience a Tirthankara preaches in the samavasarana, a hall open to all, where gods, humans and animals gather to hear him, each understanding the sermon in their own language.
565.explanation: The samavasarana ('refuge to all') presents the ideal teacher as someone everyone can approach, with no being turned away.
565.tie_back: Valluvar condemns the ruler who is hard to see and scowls at those who come; the Jain image of the Jina's open assembly is its opposite, a presence anyone can reach.
565.source: Samavasarana in Jain tradition (summary in Wikipedia, 'Samavasarana')
565._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from Wikipedia as a last resort; the Kural's point about hoarded, useless wealth has no Jain counterpart here, and the contrast is indirect.

566.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
566.explanation: The text sets rough speech, which turns away even the gentle, against courtesy, which wins over even the hot-tempered.
566.tie_back: The Kural says a harsh-tongued ruler without kindly regard loses his wealth at once; the Jain verse likewise treats harsh speech as something that loses goodwill and courtesy as what earns it.
566.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
566._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The setting is pupil and teacher, and the loss of wealth is absent.

567.quote_or_event: The Tattvartha Sutra lists nine graded kinds of expiation (prayascitta) for faults, running from confession and repentance through penance and temporary suspension up to expulsion and reinitiation, so that the correction can be matched to the gravity of the fault.
567.explanation: Jain monastic discipline uses a graded scale of remedies rather than one severe penalty, starting from the mildest step of confession.
567.tie_back: The Kural says punishment beyond measure wears down a king's power like a file; the Jain scale of expiation is built on the opposite principle of measured correction.
567.source: Tattvartha Sutra 9.22 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
567._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the sutra and the Sarvarthasiddhi gloss on wisdomlib. It concerns monastic self-correction, not royal punishment, and does not say excess weakens the ruler.

568.quote_or_event: “Anger destroys love, pride destroys modesty, deceit destroys friendship; greed is destructive of everything.”
568.explanation: This verse, which comes from the Dasavaikalika Sutra, names anger as the passion (kashaya) that destroys affection.
568.tie_back: The Kural's king who rages at his counsellors instead of deliberating with them sees his fortune shrink; the Jain verse explains the mechanism, since anger destroys the goodwill his rule depends on.
568.source: Saman Suttam 135 (English tr., jainworld.com; from Dasavaikalika Sutra 8.38)
568._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Saman Suttam text on jainworld.com. It is a general teaching on the passions, with no reference to kings, counsel or loss of fortune.

569.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable”
569.explanation: When Indra urges the renouncing King Nami to build walls, gates, battlements and a moat, Nami answers that the true fortress is built from faith, self-control and patience.
569.tie_back: The Kural's king perishes because he has prepared no place of defence; Nami agrees that defence must be prepared in advance but says the fortress that really protects is inner discipline, not stone.
569.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.20-22 (cf. 9.18) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
569._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (excerpt from a longer verse group). Nami turns military defence into a spiritual metaphor, while the Kural means a literal fortress.

570.quote_or_event: “When reprimanded a wise man should not be angry, but he should be of a forbearing mood; he should not associate, laugh, and play with mean men.”
570.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana tells the disciplined person to avoid keeping company with base people.
570.tie_back: The Kural's tyrant binds the unlearned to himself as his helpers; the Jain verse warns against exactly that kind of association.
570.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
570._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It is a personal rule for a monk; the Kural's idea of the earth bearing a tyrant as a burden is absent.
